# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–34 (Updated 2026-10-13)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Summer of ninth year after Waterloo (1830). Chapter 33 spans Sunday, 26th April through following week; Chapter 34 begins summer. Chapter 33 Sunday includes house dinner at 8 PM with five or six men; gambling afterward, card-room convenes ~11 PM Sunday night.
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Langham Hotel, Euston Square Railway Station, Bruton Street, Lincoln's Inn, Queen's Gate); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Pumpernickel; Ostend; Hampshire ("the Evergreens"); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Carbury Hall; Carbury Chase; Caversham; Sussex; Quenwick; Dunholt village; Salford; Sheepstone; Bungay; Sheep's Acre Farm; Sheepstone Birches; Yarlton; Staveton; Fenmere hill farms; Suffolk; New York; San Francisco; Liverpool; Harrowgate; Mirecombe.

## Major Deaths
- **John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt**: All deceased as previously documented.

## Rebecca's Arc
- Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon, young baronet) receives liberal allowance but declines to see her. Appears very wealthy at Bath and Cheltenham. Busies herself in piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
- Married at Dike (Ostend); Amelia initiated encounter in "dripping white bonnet and shawl." Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; fonder of daughter Jane than of his History of the Punjaub.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Lives on Welbeck Street with Felix and Henrietta. Authored "Criminal Queens." Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review by Mr. Jones (Mr. Alf's reviewer); praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" review by Mr. Broune. Suspects Alf orders hostile reviews of friends' works. Proposed scheme: if Henrietta married Roger, Felix could inherit his name, title, property. Felix consented to remain at Manor House. At Monday Caversham dinner, found Melmotte "heavy on her hands." Urged Felix to formally propose to Marie's father, warning: "don't put it off; you don't know how many slips there may be between the cup and the lip." Felix refused, claiming awkwardness.

**Felix Carbury**: Beautiful; cynosure of mother's eyes. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough, £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming. Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company. **Sunday, 26th April: Found Madame Melmotte, Marie, Georgiana Longestaffe, and Lord Nidderdale in drawing-room. Marie fell asleep; secretly instructed Felix to find Melmotte in book-room below. Melmotte assumed Felix came about railway shares and resolved to be stern, employing strategy of intimidating through assumed superiority or cultivating cupidity; prefers young associates as more timid and less greedy. When Melmotte questioned his income, Felix lacked courage to speak truth. Melmotte, puzzled by English peerage system, questioned how baronet could be heir to Esquire. Felix walked to club afterward feeling checkmated, full of wrath, unable to stand against Melmotte. After house dinner Sunday night (7 PM), approached Dolly Longestaffe for cash, urgently needing to "take up a lot of shares in the city to-morrow; or perhaps Wednesday might do," claiming Melmotte said only objection to him and Marie's marriage was money. In smoking-room, attempted business with Miles Grendall (Secretary), beginning with unusual courtesy. When Grendall remained impassive, Felix grew angry, demanding in whisper: "Then, when the deuce will you pay me what you owe me?" Sunday night card-room (~11 PM): Doubted propriety of joining party with man seeming liberated from obligation to pay, but needed gambling table. Sat next to Grendall, observed him moving chair away. Became moderate in play, tossing cards, almost always losing, watching board. Lost minimum.** **Monday afternoon at club: Read Marie's letter (see below); turned up nose, shook head, deemed much of "that kind of thing" intolerable even with marriage and money certain; crumpled letter muttering "What an infernal little ass!"**

**Marie Melmotte to Felix** (letter, delivered via Didon with gift of gloves and shoes): "Papa is very cross to her [mamma] sometimes...if he does [beat me], I'll bear it,—for your sake...I will never,--never give you up...Do write and tell me that you love me...You can come and call,--unless papa tells the man in the hall not to let you in...Papa dined out yesterday with that Lord Alfred, so I haven't seen him since you were here."

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit, claiming too young and age disparity insurmountable. Within week, Paul returned "as a still dear friend," promising not to see her three months. Wore rose from Roger's room. When met Roger at door, there was "more in her eyes of graciousness towards him than he had ever seen there before." Roger declared love anew (Chapter 32 evening); Henrietta has not committed; Roger's determination remains unshaken.

## Ruby Ruggles
- Granddaughter of old Daniel Ruggles, of Sheep's Acre, parish of Sheepstone, near Bungay. Pretty with long glossy ringlets, large round dark eyes, clear dark complexion; strong, healthy, tall; possessed own will. Had been to marry John Crumb (marriage abandoned/postponed). Understood degradation must be avoided. After Sunday meeting with Felix, resolved: "I suppose I am to be his wedded wife...I'll never be nothing unless I'm that."

## The Melmottes

**Augustus Melmotte**: Chairman of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company. Arrived London from Paris within two years; claims English birth but speaks with accent betraying "long expatriation." Big man with large whiskers, rough hair; expression of mental power on harsh vulgar face. In City, his name "worth any money." Taken up old Longestaffe's affairs; has Caversham and Sussex property. Miles Grendall serves as usher/secretary. **By Chapter 33 Board day, has twice sold fifty shares at £112 10s., receiving cheques for £625 each (£25 profit per share above £100 nominal). During Whitsun week country visit, remained in summer-house with Lord Alfred, smoking, drinking brandy and seltzer, appearing not in good humour.** **Believed by Montague to be "as vile a scoundrel as ever lived."**

**Marie Melmotte**: Speaks English well; has begun forming own opinions. Rejected Lord Grasslough; has experience with Lord Nidderdale. Currently pursued by Sir Felix Carbury (claimed favourite in London). **Sunday: Fell asleep in chair before fire caught. Secretly instructed Felix to find father in book-room, telling him "Papa is down-stairs in the book-room. Lord Alfred was told when he came that he was out." Resolved on constancy toward Felix; rejected other suitors. Felt complete happiness; promised to tell mother. Blushes when Felix mentioned, fearing his faithlessness. Monday: Entrusted letter to Didon with little present of gloves and shoes; went down to breakfast with mother and Miss Longestaffe.**

**Madame Melmotte**: Gracious as usual but never very gracious. Called Miss Longestaffe "a great bore" and "fatigante." Dismissed Marie's declarations of caring. Appears to know of Felix's offer; does not absolutely disapprove. Miss Longestaffe found her bad but silent; she seemed to understand her guest was "only her guest as a matter of business." Melmotte kept himself very much apart from Miss Longestaffe; she met him only at dinner, and that not often.

## The Longestaffes

**Sir Merton Longestaffe**: Determined no more London expenses that year; family will not return from Caversham. Desires to sell Pickering and disembarrass Caversham from debt. Dolly refused to consent unless half produce given to him. Broke promise to Georgiana of returning to London. **Chapter 34: Received letter (from Dolly, marvellous to him that his son should have been instigated to write) like a thunderbolt. The Melmottes must be "very bad indeed,--worse than he had thought." Most angered by passage telling him he ought to have taken family back to town—from his son who had refused to help him in his difficulties.**

**Georgiana Longestaffe**: Made strong protest against Melmottes; threatened to stay in London. Father refused; she felt "treachery." Meditated revenge: "I will do something. I'm not going to be cheated and swindled." Most angered that family "should have condescended to be civil to the Melmottes down in the country." Following morning, Lady Pomona handed her undated invitation from Melmotte to stay with them. Breathed very hard; noted insolence. Questioned mother. Expressed contempt for Melmottes, calling them vulgar. Yet concluded: "I'll go." **Friday morning before departure to railway station, conversation with younger sister Sophia was "almost touching." Georgiana failed to hold up her head as usual; cowed. Told Sophia: "Sophy, I do so envy you staying here."** **By Sunday, present at Grosvenor Square drawing-room with Madame Melmotte, Marie, and Lord Nidderdale, carrying on flirtation with Nidderdale in half whisper, wholly indifferent to hostess or young lady of house.** **Chapter 34: Now staying with Melmottes in Grosvenor Square. Dependent on Madame Melmotte for carriage outings and access to social parties.**

**Sophia Longestaffe**: Younger Miss. Somewhat reconciled to country sojourn as it inflicted fitting punishment on Georgiana and because Mr. Whitstable's proximity made difference.

**Adolphus (Dolly) Longestaffe**: Has own rooms in Bruton Street; seldom dines with family. Obdurate regarding his own rights in property dealings. Sunday evening sauntered into Beargarden at ~7 PM seeking sherry and bitters; present at house dinner and card-room gambling. **Chapter 34: Called on his sister at Melmotte house—declared at once he did not wish to see Madame Melmotte or any family, only Georgiana. Arrival remarkable; his mind must have been "much stirred" to be moved to such "uncommon action." Came very early hour, not much after noon, when custom to eat breakfast in bed. Georgiana complained of confinement: "How should you like to be shut up down at Caversham all the season?"**

**Lady Pomona**: Complained of headache at Caversham; slept through afternoon's tension.

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme

**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City, branching from San Francisco and Chicago line, passing through New Mexico and Arizona into Mexico, terminating at Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles. Fisker considers cost questions "beside the mark and childish." Concession obtained from United States Government.

**Financial Strategy**: Stock at par; shares sold at premium to "run them up even to 110," yielding three hundred thousand dollars minimum. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not making actual railway.

**London Directorate**: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury, Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague.

**Fisker's Departure**: Started Saturday morning, 19th April. Met by Nidderdale and Montague.

## Paul Montague and Mrs. Hurtle
Living at Beargarden. Junior member of railway firm; English. Personally dislikes Fisker but unable to resist his combination. Trembles for his money. Entertained Lord Alfred once; dined twice with Melmotte in Grosvenor Square. Saw good deal of Sir Felix, Lord Nidderdale; champagne consumption increased. Could not wake up on London mornings with satisfactory thoughts as at Carbury Hall. **Sunday night card-room: Present at gambling; won heavily from him by Grendall in run of luck.**

**Chapter 34—The Woman from America**: Woman (Mrs. Hurtle) formerly betrothed to Paul arrived night before last (Tuesday reached Liverpool, came to London Wednesday). During earlier engagement, he told her he was "going to see what he could make of his broken fortunes,—for at this time...there was no great railway in existence,—and she had promised to follow him." He had seen her in New York on second journey to San Francisco, renewed promises despite cousin's caution. Since then never met until this day. She had not made promised journey to San Francisco before he left it. Letters from her reached him in England; he answered explaining engagement must end. She has now followed him to London. **Conversations at Harrowgate location**: She said: "I could not get across to San Francisco as I said I would, and when I was there you had quarrelled with your uncle and returned." When he told her "Things are changed," she threw herself on knees: "Paul, I have come again across the Atlantic on purpose to see you,--after so many months,--and will you not give me one kiss?" He kissed her, embraced her warmly, wished she had remained away but could not refuse her. She said: "I at any rate have been faithful." She was penniless at New York meeting but "I have got my own now out from the very teeth of robbers." **Montague believes his position perfectly indefensible. He made up his mind to break engagement before seeing Henrietta Carbury; knows rumours of Mrs. Hurtle's past life and harbours uncertainty about her husband (whether he is alive). He intends to marry Henrietta, not Mrs. Hurtle, but cannot articulate reasons without admitting himself false, perjured, inconstant, and base. Mrs. Hurtle demands answer and challenges him: if he denies her statement to Madame Melmotte (whom she has already told she is Paul's promised wife, backed by his letters), he must publicly call her a liar. Paul prepared to leave without clarifying the matter.**

## Lord Nidderdale
Intent on marrying Marie Melmotte for her fortune. Claims not afraid of Melmotte, believing Melmotte "rather likes me, because I've always been on the square with him," asserting "If it depended on him, you know, I should have the girl to-morrow." On Friday Board day, walked with Melmotte to Abchurch Lane offices, asking about his position regarding shares. Melmotte told him to wait, shares would be allocated but not transferable until he qualifies by investing "a few thousand pounds." **Sunday drawing-room: Flirting with Miss Longestaffe in half whisper, wholly indifferent to hostess or young lady of house. Sunday night: Present at card-room gambling; objected to loo but capitulated.**

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty years old. Never owed shilling he could not pay; father likewise. Firmly opposed to Melmotte connection on principle; holds old-fashioned idea that "touching of pitch will defile." Took degree at Oxford; became "pervert," supposed "convert." Works as priest earning day-labourer's wages; forced to buy second-hand clothes. Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless, yet condemns himself for harsh words. During Sunday evening with Father Barham, engaged in theological debate; became tired of priest's intolerance. Later showed courtesy as host despite disapproval of Melmotte scheme. Declared love to Henrietta anew (Chapter 32 evening); determination remains unshaken.

## Father John Barham
Priest of Beccles. Dogmatic Catholic; believes man should abandon reason to care of another or others. Faith sufficient unto itself. In county only twelve months; knew nearly every Roman Catholic's name within borders.

## Property Relations
**Daniel Ruggles' Land**: Holds Sheep's Acre Farm on bishop's lease, part of property which belonged to bishopric of Elmham. Also holds small extent of outlying meadow belonging to Carbury estate; thus one of Roger Carbury's tenants. Sheepstone Birches (wood/copse) belonged to Roger.

## Other Characters
- **Miles Grendall**: Secretary/usher to Melmotte. Does not pay debts of honour; made no answer regarding repayment; lacks impudence to avoid discussing business while accepting that private matters separate from affairs of business. **Sunday card-room: Won heavily, particularly from Paul Montague; destroyed paper counters representing £1,000+; received considerable ready money "quite a godsend to him." When pressed by Felix about debt, rose and suggested billiards, walking slowly out of room, leaving Felix to take what revenge he pleased. Felix feared Grendall was more popular man than himself and did not expose transaction to whole room. During hour of play, observed moving chair farther from Felix and nearer to Dolly.**
- **Lord Grasslough**: Present at Sunday card-room gambling.
- **Unidentified narrative fragments** (Feten Lindner, Aessa Hollwood, Neena, Orric Wexwood, Rira Stenworth, Pebin Wexwood, Breena Orlwood, Red Jovus): Characters and scenes appearing interspersed throughout Chapter 34 without clear narrative integration or immediate plot connection. Include actions in Harrowgate, Yarlton, Mirecombe contexts. Status and function unclear—may be errors, drafts, or alternative narrative threads. Pebin and Breena appear to be in same location; Rira moved from Harrowgate to Yarlton; Red Jovus followed her.
